songs.title: The Spare Key on the Fridge
songs.intendedFeel: slow two-step pulse; relaxed syncopation; sustained open vowels

lines: You left a spare key where the magnets make a line,
Between the grocery list and a faded paper sign.
We never made a ceremony out of coming through the door,
We learned the sound of footsteps on the old upstairs floor.
One night the hallway filled with boxes stacked in rows,
You held the smallest lamp and asked which way the sofa goes.
I didn't know the answer, and you laughed without a sound,
Then set the lamp beside the chair and knelt to clear the ground.
The windows don't fit perfectly, the cupboard doesn't close,
But you know which loose floorboard creaks before the kettle goes.
Leave the light where we can find it,
Leave a little room beside it.
If the day gets loud and long,
There's a quiet place where we belong.
In April we were arguing about a coat left in the rain,
You went outside to get it while I counted every stain.
You came back with a photograph you'd found below the stair,
Two strangers in this kitchen from a year we weren't here.
They'd written on the border, "Keep the table if you can,"
So we sanded down the scratches with a borrowed little fan.
You signed beneath the picture in your unambitious hand,
And called the narrow kitchen something close to what we'd planned.
Keep the light where we can find it,
Set a bigger table by it.
When the day gets loud and long,
There's more than room for us to belong.
The spare key on the fridge door hardly shines against the white,
But I turn it in the lock and know that someone left a light.
Not a promise that the weather or the years will all be kind—
Just a place to put our burdens and a door we chose to find.

songs.title: The Platform Is a Drum
songs.intendedFeel: alternating call-response, percussion-first pocket, group refrain

lines: LEAD: A bucket and a bench—who brought the beat?
GROUP: The baker from the corner with the flour on his feet.
LEAD: Who found the backbeat hiding under station four?
GROUP: The guard who shuts the shutters when he closes up the door.
DANCER: I mark the stones in patterns while the evening buses stall.
My left foot keeps the high notes; my right can catch the fall.
You tell me I should stand still when the traffic lights turn red—
But a pause is just a doorway for the next beat in my head.
DRUMMER: My brother taught me rhythm with a pencil and a tin.
I learned to hear the spaces where the quieter drums begin.
Don't need a wall of thunder if the pocket has a place;
I let the final snare hit twice, then leave the room some space.
GROUP: Tap the rail, answer back.
GROUP: Hear the wheel upon the track.
LEAD: One small sound can start the floor.
GROUP: Leave some room for one beat more.
VIOLINIST: The strings can float above it with a note that bends and leans.
I start outside the downbeat, then pull across their feet.
The drummer drops to silence; now my bow can barely sing—
He catches my last whisper with a soft tap on the rim.
GUARD: The final bus is pulling up. The driver shakes his head.
He says the neighbors need their sleep; the hour's past the end.
LEAD: We nod and pack the instruments, then move toward the square;
The rhythm takes the staircase, but the platform keeps the air.
GROUP: Tap the rail, then let it rest.
LEAD: The quiet part is not a test.
ALL: Tomorrow has another track.
ALL: And every echo carries back.

songs.title: The Little Window Upstairs
songs.intendedFeel: gentle three-pulse or 6/8 sway; lyric doesn't assert performed meter

lines: A little window upstairs,
A ribbon caught in the breeze,
The city folds away its noise
Among the sleeping trees.
Your blanket holds the moonlight
In squares upon the wall,
And somewhere in the courtyard
The latest raindrops fall.
Rest, little wanderer, rest,
The street can find its way.
The trains will take their journeys;
You can save yours for the day.
The neighbor turns a page,
A kettle settles down,
The washing lines are holding
The softest shirts in town.
No one needs an answer,
No race must yet be run;
A dream can take the long way
And still arrive with sun.
Sleep, little wanderer, sleep,
The windows know the rain.
The trains can keep their journeys;
You'll have your own again.
One lamp beneath the curtain,
One hand beside your hand,
A quiet little harbor
No map has ever planned.

songs.title: Room for the Fifth Beat
songs.intendedFeel: intended five-count phrasing on selected hook lines, variable resets; not audio-confirmed

lines: Every room in the warehouse is marked with chalk,
Every footstep echoes when the night crew walks.
One light flickers twice, then it waits for a third,
And the concrete keeps the shape of an unfinished word.
I count the steps from loading bay to painted door,
There used to be four; now the workers count one more.
The clock still tells us when to close the steel outside,
But nothing here explains why the echo will not hide.
One, two—hold it—three, four, five.
Leave the quiet part alive.
One, two—turn it—three, four, five.
That's the sound of getting by.
The oldest night watch walks the corridor alone,
Picks up an empty cup beside the telephone.
He taps the steel handrail where the ceiling lights go dark,
And hears a second answer from beyond the loading park.
He finds a loose board banging on the outer gate,
And tightens two old screws before it gets too late.
When the machinery returns to its ordinary chime,
The missing little silence feels as strange as missing time.
Count less.
Listen more.
Hear the hinges
On the door.
Breathe once.
Wait and see—
No floor can hold a rhythm
If it leaves no room for me.
One, two—let go—three, four, five.
Leave the quiet part alive.
One, two—slow down—three, four, five.
Now the whole room feels alive.

songs.title: Inventory of Things Not Said
songs.intendedFeel: asymmetric speech rhythm, sparse internal sound recurrence, silence as a choice
techniques: object list that becomes an argument
perspective turn without a repeated hook

lines: There is a receipt
in the drawer beside the sink.
It says we bought six cups.
Only five remain.
There is an umbrella
that has forgotten its owner,
a calendar turned to March
though the hallway is already warm.
I used to think the things we didn't say
had no weight.
Then I tried to carry a cardboard box
full of folded letters
up three flights of stairs,
and the bottom opened
halfway to the landing.
Nothing spectacular happened.
I knelt.
I gathered the papers.
A neighbor held the door
without asking who had written them.
There is a kind of mercy
in a question
that never needs to be spoken.
The receipt is still in the drawer.
I bring the remaining cups
down to the kitchen table,
and make room for one more.

songs.title: Paint on the Dance Floor
songs.intendedFeel: short hook, clipped accent lines, propulsive dance groove, call-and-response

lines: The old hall's got a scuff on the boards,
A line of blue tape and a stack of awards.
Somebody brought a bass in a box from the train,
Somebody brought a towel for the windows in the rain.
The caretaker points at a patch by the wall,
Says, "That's where the paint won't come off at all."
We step around the patch till the drummer hits two,
Then all of the shoes leave the tape for the blue.
Step left—hold tight.
Hands up—feet light.
Don't paint the room.
Let the room paint the night.
The sax finds a note in the corner by the fan,
The keys drop a chord when the cymbal says it can.
One shoe keeps the one beat, the other finds three,
The whole little floor learns a new geometry.
The caretaker smiles, though he swore he wouldn't dance,
His mop has a handle like a partner at the chance.
He spins it through the doorway as the bass comes around,
And a blue-tape border turns to part of the sound.
No trophies.
No parade.
Just the small new
Steps we made.
One bass note—
Take your place.
Catch the corner,
Turn your face.
Step left—let go.
Hands up—move slow.
We didn't paint the room.
The room gave us somewhere to go.

songs.title: The Parcel Route
songs.intendedFeel: bursts of internal assonance punctuated by short end-stop lines; no exact BPM claims

lines: Stacking the packets and tracking the addresses,
Back through the passages, checking the messages.
Every new label is faded or crooked,
One little barcode was smudged when they took it.
Flip it. Read twice. Mark the lane.
There's a late-route van in the hammering rain.
Clocking the loading, unloading the corners,
Sorting the parcels for sleepy shop owners.
A box with a violin hums when it moves,
Another holds seedlings in paper-wrapped tubes.
Fragile—not because the sticker says so,
But because somebody cares where its contents will go.
Across the canal where the tall buildings narrow,
A woman chalks arrows on boards by a barrow.
Follow the footbridge, then circle the station,
Don't take the service gate under construction.
I pivot, I listen, I shift my attention,
A sign on the fence has an old contradiction:
ONE WAY points east, but the bridge runs to west,
So I stop at the corner and put it to test.
Ten steps. Check the curb. Find the stairs.
There's a green-painted doorway with three folding chairs.
The violin's owner is waiting in silence,
She opens the case and checks each string's winding.
She plays one short note; in the hallway it lingers,
Then draws out the next with a tremor of fingers.
Back to the depot, the wheels start their clatter,
Loose little pebbles are hitting the ladder.
A driver is arguing, "Nothing is moving!"
I say, "Check the map," and show him what we're losing:
Every wrong arrow steals time from a neighbor,
Every sharp turn asks for patience and labor.
Not fame. Not glory. Just doing the route.
Find the right address. Bring the right parcel out.
A child brings the seedlings onto a balcony ledge,
And a little green leaf turns beside the concrete edge.
I leave the last package with a note on its string,
Then the warehouse alarm starts its late-evening ring.
Hurry can help when it's honest and measured;
Speed without purpose is noise without treasure.

songs.title: The Woven Sail
songs.intendedFeel: acoustic storyteller, understated recurring couplet, broad 6/8 feel not verified

lines: An old sailmaker lived above the market by the pier,
She kept a box of sea-worn thread and every sailor's year.
Her fingers knew the shape of storms before the clouds could show,
She'd stitch a narrow seam and tell the young ones where to go.
One morning came a fishing boat with canvas split in three,
The captain said the season's end was coming with the sea.
She took the torn white cloth and laid it over by the door,
Then swept away the sand from all the sails upon the floor.
Hold the thread, keep the line.
Give the weather room and time.
One good seam can hold till dawn;
One new hand can carry on.
A girl who swept the workshop asked to hold the needle straight,
The sailmaker said, "You can learn, but you will have to wait."
She showed her how the fabric pulls against a sudden gale,
And why a patch that looks too neat can make a weaker sail.
They worked until the evening, when the harbor lamps came on,
Then carried out the canvas with the shape of night upon.
The captain took the repaired sail and pointed toward the bay,
The girl said she was frightened it would split another day.
Hold the thread, trust the line.
Give your hands another time.
One good seam may hold till dawn;
One new hand can carry on.
The first cold squall arrived before the little fleet reached land,
A signal rose above the boats, then turned to wave and sand.
The sailmaker stood waiting where the lighthouse faced the shore,
And saw the stitched white canvas find its shape against the roar.
By morning every fishing boat had found its mooring place,
She saw her stitching holding where the canvas met the brace.
They hung the weathered sail to dry and drank their cups of tea,
The old hands gave the needle to the girl beside the sea.
